content:
Yesterday we saw Miriam and Aaron speak against Moses. Their spoken complaint was about his Cushite wife, but the deeper problem was jealousy and pride over his unique authority. Yahweh heard every word, called all three of them to the Tabernacle, and descended in the pillar of cloud. He had just begun to explain that He speaks to ordinary prophets through dreams and visions.
We ended there, as Yahweh was about to say something about Moses that Miriam and Aaron desperately needed to hear.

Numbers 12:7-8 gives us those words. "But not with my servant Moses. Of all my house, he is the one I trust. I speak to him face to face, clearly, and not in riddles! He sees the LORD as he is. So why were you not afraid to criticize my servant Moses?" Yahweh called Moses "my servant." He said Moses was faithful in all His house. He did not speak to Moses only through dreams and visions, as with other prophets. He spoke to him directly, clearly, and not in riddles. And then Yahweh asked the piercing question that lay at the very heart of the matter: "Why were you not afraid to criticize my servant Moses?"

Miriam and Aaron had not merely criticized a family member. They had spoken against Yahweh's appointed servant, and they should have trembled before ever speaking in such a way.

Numbers 12:9 says, "Yahweh was very angry with them, and he departed." Yahweh's anger was kindled, and the cloud moved away from the Tabernacle. And immediately, judgment appeared. Numbers 12:10 says, "As the cloud moved from above the Tabernacle, there stood Miriam, her skin as white as snow from leprosy. When Aaron saw what had happened to her..." Miriam was struck with a skin disease like leprosy, and her skin became white as snow. Aaron saw what had happened and immediately understood the seriousness of what they had done. It is important to notice that Miriam alone was struck with this condition. This may show that she was the main one who began the complaint, especially because her name is mentioned first in Numbers 12:1. Aaron was guilty too, but Miriam received the visible punishment.

Then Aaron spoke to Moses. Numbers 12:11-12 says, "He cried out to Moses, 'Oh, my master! Please don't punish us for this sin we have so foolishly committed. Don't let her be like a stillborn baby, already decayed at birth.'

Leprosy or severe skin disease made Miriam’s skin appear white and diseased. Aaron felt it looked like death had already touched her body. So he pleads with Moses not to let her become like someone already dead and wasting away. Aaron confessed that they had acted foolishly and had sinned. He did not defend himself any longer. He did not continue the argument. He simply pleaded with Moses to help Miriam. And this is striking. The same Aaron who had joined in criticizing Moses now turned to Moses and asked for mercy.The very one they had spoken against became the one they now needed.And Moses, for his part, did not rejoice in Miriam's punishment. He did not say, "Now she has learned her lesson." Numbers 12:13 says, "So Moses cried out to the LORD, 'O God, I beg you, please heal her!'" He immediately cried out to Yahweh for her healing. This shows us the humility and the mercy of Moses. Though he had been criticized, he interceded for the very one who had spoken against him.

Yahweh answered Moses, but He did not remove the discipline immediately. Numbers 12:14 says, "But the LORD said to Moses, 'If her father had done nothing more than spit in her face, wouldn't she be defiled for seven days?

So keep her outside the camp for seven days, and after that she may be accepted back.'" This statement may sound difficult at first. But this was not a law commanding fathers to spit on their daughters. There is no law of Moses saying such a thing. Yahweh was using a familiar picture of shame and severe rebuke. In those times, spitting in someone's face was a strong sign of disgrace, contempt, and public shame. Deuteronomy 25:9 speaks of a public act of disgrace in which a woman spat in the face of a man who refused his duty.Job 30:10 says Job's enemies did not hesitate to spit in his face. Isaiah 50:6 speaks of the suffering servant who did not hide his face from shame and spitting.And Matthew 26:67 tells us that the enemies of our Master spat in his face to humiliate him. So Yahweh's point was this: if even an earthly father's public rebuke would bring shame for seven days, how much more should Miriam accept the discipline of her heavenly Father? She had sinned publicly by speaking against Moses, so her correction was also public. Yet Yahweh did not permanently reject her. Her punishment was serious, but it was temporary.The seven days also connect with the period of examination and exclusion for a suspected skin disease, for Leviticus 13:4 says, "The priest will put the infected person in quarantine for seven days."

Numbers 12:15 says, "So Miriam was kept outside the camp for seven days, and the people waited until she was brought back before they traveled again."

This shows us both discipline and mercy together. Miriam had to bear the shame of being shut outside the camp. And the whole nation had to wait for her. Her sin affected far more than herself. Her criticism actually delayed the journey of all Israel. But after seven days, she was restored. Yahweh corrected her, but He did not cast her away forever. Numbers 12:16 concludes, "Then they left Hazeroth and camped in the wilderness of Paran." After Miriam was brought back, Israel continued the journey. The chapter ends with movement again. The discipline was completed, restoration took place, and the camp moved forward.

So Numbers chapter twelve teaches us the seriousness of speaking against the servant whom Yahweh has appointed. Miriam and Aaron began by criticizing Moses' marriage, but Yahweh exposed the deeper issue. Their real complaint was about authority and position, for they had asked, "Has Yahweh spoken only through Moses? Has He not spoken through us also?" Jealousy and ambition can sometimes hide behind another complaint. A person may speak as though the issue is moral, spiritual, or practical, but God sees what is truly in the heart. In this case the spoken issue was Moses' wife, but the hidden issue was pride and rebellion against Moses' unique calling. God defended Moses. He showed that Moses was faithful in His house and that He spoke with Moses in an exceptional way. Miriam was judged with a skin disease, Aaron confessed their foolish sin, Moses interceded, God gave discipline, and after seven days Miriam was restored. This whole chapter stands as a serious reminder.
God hears private criticism. God sees hidden pride. God knows when jealousy is hiding behind a complaint. But Yahweh is also merciful. When Moses prayed, Miriam was healed, and when the discipline was complete, she was brought back into the camp. There is a deeper spiritual meaning in all of this for us, the New Creation, and God willing, we will study its spiritual meaning tomorrow.

title: Prayer
text:
My God,

We thank You for the warning and the mercy shown in this chapter.

Help us to fear You before we ever speak against those whom You have appointed.

Keep our hearts free from jealousy, from pride, and from hidden ambition.

Make us humble like Moses, quick to pray for others and slow to defend ourselves.

And we thank You that even when You discipline, You also restore.

"He does not deal harshly with us, as we deserve, nor repay us according to our sins." - Psalm 103:10

In the name of Christ, we pray. Amen.
